summary: This document defines an SDP attribute for the delay between duplicated packets in time-shifted redundancy. Sending each packet twice, separated in time by at least T, protects against losses from outages lasting up to T.

eli5.summary: Send the same note twice, a little apart, so if one gets lost in a bump the other still arrives. This lets the sender say how far apart.

questions: what is the sdp duplication-delay attribute
what is temporal redundancy in rtp
how does delayed duplication protect against packet loss
subtitle: An SDP attribute that says how long to wait before sending each duplicate copy of a media packet.

tldr.problem: Sending every packet twice, a little apart in time, can protect real-time media from short network outages, but receivers need to be told that streams are duplicates and how far apart the copies are.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7197 defines the SDP attribute 'duplication-delay', which lists the delay in milliseconds of each duplicate relative to the previous transmission. It works together with the DUP grouping semantics of RFC 7104.
tldr.outcome: A sender can announce time-shifted redundancy in SDP for RTP and non-RTP streams. The RFC does not say how to pick the delay or how to merge the streams.

facts.label: Delay unit
facts.value: Milliseconds, relative to the previous transmission

today: RFC 7197 is a Proposed Standard from April 2014 and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It is used together with RFC 7104 and RFC 7198.

sections.title: Why Send Packets Twice
sections.content:
When a link, interface or device fails, packets are dropped until the network reconverges around the failure. The RFC says this typically takes tens to hundreds of milliseconds. Network-level fast-reroute technologies can be combined with application-layer loss repair such as Forward Error Correction (FEC), retransmission, temporal redundancy and spatial redundancy.

This document is about temporal redundancy, also called delayed duplication or time-shifted redundancy. The sender transmits each packet and then sends a duplicate after a delay. If an outage hits the original, the duplicate probably arrives. If both arrive, the receiver, or a node doing duplicate suppression, discards the extra copy.

Compared with FEC and redundant data encoding, the RFC says delayed duplication is easy to implement because it needs no special encoding or decoding.
sections.eli5: If a bump in the road can knock one parcel off the truck, you send a second identical parcel a bit later. At least one is likely to get through.

sections.title: Where Duplication Helps and Where It Hurts
sections.content:
Delayed duplication suits multimedia applications that have enough spare bandwidth for the extra traffic and can tolerate the added delay. A particular use case is real-time video feeds inside a core IP network where bandwidth is plentiful and zero loss is preferred.

It must be used with care. It is harmful when the main cause of loss is congestion rather than a temporary link or network element failure, because duplicates only make congestion worse. The RFC also warns that it might easily create a new series of denial-of-service attacks.

The receiver must be able to spot identical packets. For RTP this is easy because of the sequence number in the RTP header. For non-RTP traffic the receiver can use unique sequence numbers if they exist, or other ways to compare packets. In practice, more than two redundant streams are unlikely, but the attribute is defined generally so it can describe more.
sections.eli5: Sending extra copies is great when a bump knocks one off, but if the road is simply jammed with traffic, more copies just make the jam worse.

sections.title: The duplication-delay Attribute
sections.content:
The duplication-delay attribute carries one or more periods, each a string of digits in milliseconds. Each period is the relative delay of one duplicate with respect to the previous transmission, at the time of transmission.

It can be used at two levels:

  • Media level: it MUST be used with the ssrc-group attribute and the DUP grouping semantics from RFC 7104. The delay values apply to every SSRC-based duplication group in that media description, so different groups in one media description cannot have different delays.
  • Session level: it MUST be used with the group attribute and DUP semantics. The values apply to every duplication group in the whole SDP description. To use different delays for different groups, use separate SDP descriptions or use the media-level attribute, and in that case the session-level attribute MUST NOT be used.

For offer/answer model considerations, the RFC points to RFC 7104.
sections.eli5: You can write the waiting time on one sticker for a single package, or on one sticker for the whole shipment. If different packages need different waits, you cannot use the whole-shipment sticker.

sections.title: SDP Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three examples. In the first, a multicast stream has two RTP streams, each duplicated once, so there are two two-stream groups. SSRCs 1000 and 1010 form the first group and 1020 and 1030 the second, and the same 100 ms delay applies to both.

In the second, a stream is duplicated twice with a=duplication-delay:50 100. The first duplicate goes 50 ms after the original and the second goes 100 ms after that, so the same packet is sent three times over 150 ms.

In the third, a multicast UDP stream is duplicated with a 50 ms delay, using a=group:DUP S1a S1b. The two copies travel in separate source-specific multicast sessions, so a receiving host has to join both to get both streams.

The RFC notes that real SSRC values are random 32-bit numbers and could be much larger than the examples.
sections.eli5: One example sends a copy once after a short wait. Another sends two copies, one after a short wait and one after a longer wait. The third sends the copy down a different pipe that the listener must also tap into.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC does not believe the attribute adds significant security risk, but lists some concerns. An attacker who can rewrite the SDP could raise the delay, making receivers wait needlessly, or lower it, so receivers do not wait long enough and lose packets. The fix is to integrity-protect and source-authenticate the SDP, for example with S/MIME, HTTPS or the authentication method of the Session Announcement Protocol.

A software bug or an attacker could signal too many duplicates and start a denial-of-service attack. The RFC advises a hard limit on both the number of duplicate streams and the total delay, whatever the SDP says.

Because duplication repeats cryptographically protected packets, it could speed up attacks such as the Million Message attack or Lucky 13 against weak mechanisms. It could also make dictionary attacks against keys derived from guessable secrets more efficient when used with SDES. The RFC says the overall impact should be minimal if duplication is small and weak mechanisms are avoided.
sections.eli5: Someone could tamper with the note and make you wait too long or too little, or trick you into sending a mountain of copies. So keep the note sealed and cap how many copies you will send.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The RFC registers a new SDP attribute (att-field) named duplication-delay. Its long form is "Duplication delay for temporally redundant streams". It can be used at media or session level, is not subject to a character set, and its purpose is to specify the relative duplication delay or delays for redundant streams.
sections.eli5: The RFC adds the new label to the official list of allowed SDP labels so nobody else uses the same name.

data.title: duplication-delay ABNF
data.code:
delaying-attribute     = "a=duplication-delay:" periods CRLF
periods                = period *( SP period)
period                 = 1*DIGIT ; in milliseconds

viz.caption: SECOND EXAMPLE: ONE PACKET SENT THREE TIMES OVER 150 MS
